          The Florian Wirtz Debate: Were Jamie Carragher’s Criticisms Harsh or Fair?
        
      
                          
                      Sep 22, 2026
          
                      David Segar / Author
                  
      
              
                      
                  
          

    
              
      
              
                    
Florian Wirtz has not had the impact many expected at Liverpool, and the criticism is getting louder. Has the Germany international really been that bad, though?
When Florian Wirtz signed for Liverpool in the summer of 2025, there was only one logical assumption.

The Premier League champions at the time had recruited one of the hottest young talents in world football, one who played a pivotal role in winning a historic double with Bayer Leverkusen in 2023-24, and was already a star of the German national team at just 22 years old.
An exciting and productive attacking midfielder being added to the best team in England? How could this not work?
Football has a habit of flipping the script, though, making the impossible possible, and ensuring that something that seems so obviously right is somehow wrong.

The 2025-26 season was difficult for several reasons at Anfield, and Wirtz, along with other new arrivals, struggled to make as much of an impact as expected for the fee agreed (£100 million + £16m in add-ons).

There were conversations among fans this summer as to how long he and fellow nine-figure signing Alexander Isak should be given before difficult questions needed be asked. The broad consensus was ‘until Christmas’.
As it turned out, the real answer was ‘after the opening game of the season’ as Wirtz and Isak laboured in Liverpool's 2-2 draw at Newcastle United and loud doubts began to surface.
Jamie Carragher spoke on the first Monday Night Football of the season about Wirtz’s signing in 2025 potentially being part of the “worst transfer window in Premier League history”.

The former Liverpool defender was criticising a few players that time – and Isak has since gone on to score four times in his last four Premier League appearances to somewhat silence his doubters – but Carragher did focus his ire solely on Wirtz on Sunday in the first episode of his new podcast for Sky Sports.

🗣️ "I don't think Florian Wirtz is in poor form, what we're seeing is what he is"Jamie Carragher says he is worried for Florian Wirtz and doesn't see how he will hurt teams ⤵️ pic.twitter.com/umgZ0ZgfzK

“The reason I worry is, I don’t think Wirtz is in poor form since he came to Liverpool. I actually think what we’re seeing is what he is,” he said. “The worry for Wirtz now is that his performances so far, or what he’s given Liverpool, is so low. Where we were expecting him was to take Liverpool to another league title, to take Liverpool to a Champions League.

“The gap he’s got to [close] to justify what people were expecting, I almost think is too big. You can’t get there. Even if he improves a bit and gets there, it’s still not what Liverpool thought they were getting.
“I think [Andoni] Iraola’s got a decision to make here. Wirtz would not be in my Liverpool team.”

Carragher particularly derided Wirtz – who has just one assist in six games this season – for his performance in Sunday’s 1-0 win at Bournemouth, labelling it “one of the poorest I've ever seen him in a Liverpool shirt.”
Reds boss Andoni Iraola was a little more generous in his review of Wirtz’s outing, though did accept when speaking to reporters that the German had struggled in the first half.
“He started the game slowly, I agree,” Iraola said. “After that first phase, I think we improved. Florian has helped us also to improve.
“Second half he was playing much better, he was finding better spots to receive and turn… I’m much more happy with his second half.”

On paper, Wirtz’s numbers from the game weren’t that bad. He created three chances, the joint-most of any Liverpool player along with Cody Gakpo, won six of his eight duels, and won possession four times: only Alexis Mac Allister (7), Ronald Araujo (6), and Jérémy Jacquet (6) did so more often for the visitors.
Perhaps we shouldn’t be saying this, being Opta and all, but data doesn’t always tell the whole story.
